title: Greedy Algorithms: When the Best Next Step Is Enough
oneLiner: Take the locally best choice and never look back: how to tell when that's safe, how to prove it with an exchange argument, and the classic cases where it fails.
keyTakeaway: A greedy algorithm is only correct when you can argue that the locally best choice is part of SOME optimal answer. The usual proof is an exchange argument: take any optimal answer, swap its first choice for the greedy one, and show it gets no worse. If you can't make that argument, try to break the greedy rule on a tiny input; one counterexample (coins {1, 3, 4} for amount 6) means you need dynamic programming instead.
explanation:
A greedy algorithm builds its answer one decision at a time, always taking the option that looks best right now (the earliest finish, the biggest coin, the cheapest edge), and never undoing a decision. That makes greedy code short and fast, usually a sort followed by one pass, O(n log n). The catch is that it's often wrong, and it looks just as convincing when it is.

Two properties make greedy correct. The greedy-choice property: some optimal solution starts with the greedy choice. Optimal substructure: after making that choice, what's left is a smaller copy of the same problem, so the same rule can keep going. Dynamic programming needs optimal substructure too; the difference is that DP tries every choice and keeps the best, while greedy commits to one without comparing.

The exchange argument is how you show the greedy-choice property. Start from any optimal solution O. If O's first choice differs from the greedy choice g, swap it for g, and show the result is still valid and no worse. Then O with g is also optimal, and you repeat the argument on the rest. For interval scheduling (keep as many non-overlapping intervals as possible), g is the interval that ends earliest: swapping it in for O's first interval can't create an overlap, because g ends no later, so everything after it in O still fits. A related proof style, "greedy stays ahead", shows that after every step the greedy partial answer is at least as good as any other, as in Jump Game, where the farthest reach after k indexes is the best anyone can have.

Where greedy fails. Coin change with coins {1, 3, 4} and amount 6: always taking the largest coin gives 4 + 1 + 1, three coins, but 3 + 3 is two. (With real-world coin systems such as {1, 5, 10, 25} greedy happens to be optimal, which is exactly why people trust it too much.) Interval scheduling with the wrong rule: "earliest start" or "shortest first" each have a small counterexample, shown below. 0/1 knapsack by value per kilo: greedy is optimal when you may take fractions of items, but with whole items it can fill the bag badly. In all three, the fix is DP: Coin Change and 0/1 Knapsack have their own lessons in the Patterns track.

A practical interview routine: state the greedy rule in one sentence; try to break it on two or three tiny inputs, including ties and extremes; if it survives, give the exchange argument out loud; if it breaks, say so and move to DP. Interviewers reward the counterexample as much as the proof. Greedy algorithms you already know include Dijkstra's shortest path (always finalise the closest unvisited node), Kruskal's minimum spanning tree (always add the cheapest edge that doesn't close a cycle), Huffman coding, and Non-overlapping Intervals in the Patterns track.
